name: Automated Mixing and Mastering
title: Automated Mixing and Mastering
answer: Automated mixing and mastering uses machine learning to set levels, equalization, compression, stereo image, and loudness for recorded music, either as assistive tools or fully autonomous processing. It covers individual tracks, stems, and full mixes, and is used by home producers, podcasters, and professional engineers. The goal is to reduce repetitive technical work while preserving or enhancing musical intent. This page sits within music composition and audio engineering, part of The Art of AI.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems typically run as cloud services or local plugins inside a digital audio workstation. Cloud mastering services accept an uploaded mix and return a processed file, while local tools run on a producer's computer using CPU or GPU. Many rely on trained neural networks that have learned from large sets of mixed and mastered audio, and some use a hybrid of rule-based DSP and learned parameters. Latency is less critical for offline mastering than for real-time mixing.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by training models on paired examples of raw and finished audio, or on large collections of commercially released tracks. A model learns to predict gain, EQ curves, compression thresholds, and other settings from spectral and temporal features of the input. Some systems let the user set a target loudness or reference track, and the model then adjusts its processing to match that target. Others operate as a chain of separate modules for tasks like de-essing, stereo widening, and limiting.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on training data, copyright, and the status of AI-assisted recordings. Many models are trained on copyrighted music, which raises questions about whether the output is a derivative work or a licensed transformation. The site currently tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, of which 18 involve AI music services, reflecting active disputes over training and output rights. Engineers should also consider whether automated mastering alters the credited human authorship of a recording, and whether a service's terms claim ownership of uploaded audio.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Automated mixing and mastering is moving toward more context-aware systems that understand genre, arrangement, and emotional intent rather than applying a fixed chain. Real-time assistive mixing inside DAWs is likely to improve, with models that suggest moves while the engineer retains control. There is also work on separating and remixing stems automatically before mastering, and on personalized loudness and translation across playback systems. The boundary between a tool and a collaborator will continue to shift as models become more interactive.
